position: both — mostly before a noun: *nuclear power*; after a verb: *the plant is nuclear*
contrast: Say NOO-klee-ur. The common American mispronunciation NOO-kyuh-lur is heard from presidents and still counts as an error.

senses.gloss: Using the energy released by splitting atoms; involving atomic weapons.
examples: The country agreed to shut down its *nuclear* weapons program.
About a fifth of US electricity comes from *nuclear* plants.
Talks on *nuclear* disarmament resumed in Geneva.

senses.gloss: Of the central core — of a cell, or of a family of parents and children.
examples: She grew up in a traditional *nuclear* family of four.
The dye stains the *nuclear* membrane of each cell.

position: both — *a nude model*; *the figures in the painting are nude*
contrast: Also a noun in art (*a Modigliani nude*) and in the phrase *in the nude*.

senses.gloss: Wearing no clothes.
examples: The class was drawing from a *nude* model.
Several of the statues are completely *nude*.

senses.gloss: Of a pale pinkish-beige color close to skin.
examples: She wore *nude* heels with the black dress.
*Nude* lipstick is back in style.

position: both — *a null result*; in law almost always in the pair *null and void*
contrast: In everyday English it lives inside the fixed phrase *null and void*. In programming *null* is a noun for an empty value.

senses.gloss: Having no legal force.
examples: The judge declared the contract *null* and void.
If you miss the deadline, the whole agreement becomes *null*.

senses.gloss: Equal to zero, or showing no effect.
examples: The experiment produced a *null* result.
Statisticians start from the *null* hypothesis.

position: both — *numb fingers*; *my lips went numb*
contrast: The *b* is silent: NUM. The forms *number* and *numbest* exist, but Americans avoid them because *number* reads as the noun — say *more numb*.

senses.gloss: Unable to feel anything in part of the body.
examples: My fingers were *numb* with cold.
The dentist waited until my jaw was completely *numb*.

senses.gloss: Unable to feel emotion, usually after a shock.
examples: She felt *numb* for weeks after the funeral.
The news left all of us *numb*.

position: both — *a numbing cold*; *the routine was numbing*

senses.gloss: Making the body lose feeling.
examples: A *numbing* wind came off the lake.
The dentist applied a *numbing* gel first.

senses.gloss: So dull or so repeated that it deadens the mind.
examples: The job was a *numbing* routine of forms and phone calls.
There is something *numbing* about the constant bad news.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a numeric code*; *the field must be numeric*
contrast: *numeric* and *numerical* mean the same thing. Computing prefers *numeric* (*a numeric keypad*); order and analysis prefer *numerical* (*numerical order*).

senses.gloss: Expressed in numbers; made of digits.
examples: The password has to contain at least one *numeric* character.
Use the *numeric* keypad on the right side of the keyboard.
That column accepts *numeric* values only.

position: both — *numerical order*; *the advantage was purely numerical*
contrast: See *numeric*. The adverb *numerically* is common in writing: *numerically superior*.

senses.gloss: Relating to numbers, or measured by them.
examples: Please file the folders in *numerical* order.
The army had a clear *numerical* advantage.
We ran a *numerical* analysis of the survey answers.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *numerous complaints*; *her awards are too numerous to list*
contrast: *numerous* counts things, so it needs a plural countable noun: *numerous problems*, never *numerous money*.

senses.gloss: Existing in large numbers; many.
examples: We received *numerous* complaints about the noise.
She has made *numerous* attempts to reach him.
Deer are far *more numerous* here than they were twenty years ago.

position: attributive only — *nutritional value*; not *the meal is nutritional*
contrast: *nutritional* is about nutrition as a subject (*nutritional information*); food that is good for you is *nutritious*. A meal is *nutritious*, never *nutritional*.

senses.gloss: Relating to nutrition and to the food value of what people eat.
examples: The label lists the *nutritional* information for one serving.
Processing strips much of the *nutritional* value out of the grain.
She has a degree in *nutritional* science.

position: both — *a nutritious breakfast*; *the soup is cheap and nutritious*
contrast: See *nutritional*. *nutritious* praises the food itself.

senses.gloss: Containing what the body needs; good for you.
examples: Oatmeal makes a cheap, *nutritious* breakfast.
Fresh vegetables are *more nutritious* than canned ones.
The district is trying to serve *nutritious* school lunches.

position: predicative only — *he's nuts*; never *a nuts idea*
contrast: Informal. Before a noun you must switch words: *a crazy idea*, not *a nuts idea*. The noun *nuts* (орехи) is a different word altogether.

senses.gloss: Crazy; not thinking sensibly.
examples: You'd be *nuts* to turn down that offer.
The noise from upstairs is driving me *nuts*.

senses.gloss: Extremely enthusiastic about something.
examples: My daughter is *nuts* about horses.
He's absolutely *nuts* for that band.

position: both — *a nutty flavor*; *the cheese tastes nutty*

senses.gloss: Tasting or smelling of nuts.
examples: The bread has a warm, *nutty* flavor.
This coffee is *nuttier* than the one we had yesterday.

senses.gloss: Slightly crazy — informal and usually affectionate.
examples: He has some *nutty* ideas about money.
Her *nutty* uncle shows up every Thanksgiving.

position: both — *oafish behavior*; *he was loud and oafish*

senses.gloss: Behaving like a clumsy, rude, stupid man.
examples: His *oafish* jokes made everyone at the table uncomfortable.
She apologized for her brother's *oafish* behavior.
The character is written as a big, *oafish* bully.

position: both — *an obedient dog*; *the children were obedient*

senses.gloss: Doing what you are told to do.
examples: They trained the puppy to be *obedient*.
He was a quiet, *obedient* student who never caused trouble.
Soldiers are expected to be *obedient* to orders.

position: both — *obese patients*; *he was clinically obese*
contrast: A medical word. Said of a person you know it sounds blunt or cruel — *overweight* is the everyday word.

senses.gloss: So overweight that health is at risk.
examples: The doctor told him he was clinically *obese*.
The program helps *obese* children get more exercise.
The share of *obese* adults has risen sharply since the 1980s.

position: both — *objectionable content*; *the ad was objectionable*

senses.gloss: Likely to offend people or make them protest.
examples: Several parents found the book *objectionable*.
The site removes *objectionable* content within a day.
He said nothing *objectionable*, but the tone was all wrong.

position: both — *an objective report*; *try to stay objective*
contrast: *objective* is also a noun meaning a goal: *our main objective this quarter*. Same spelling, different word class.

senses.gloss: Not influenced by personal feelings; fair.
examples: It's hard to be *objective* about your own children.
We need an *objective* review from someone outside the team.

senses.gloss: Based on facts that exist independently of anyone's opinion.
examples: There is no *objective* evidence that the drug works.
The test gives an *objective* measure of reading level.

position: predicative only — *you're not obligated to answer*; never *an obligated guest*
contrast: *obligated* is the American form for a duty you actually have. *obliged* covers the same ground and adds the sense 'grateful'. Neither one goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: Having a legal or moral duty to do something.
examples: You are not *obligated* to say anything without a lawyer.
I felt *obligated* to invite her.
The company is legally *obligated* to notify customers.

position: both — *an obligatory course*; *attendance is obligatory*
contrast: Often used jokingly for the thing everybody always does: *the obligatory family photo*.

senses.gloss: Required by a rule or by custom.
examples: A first-aid class is *obligatory* for all new staff.
Attendance at the Monday meeting is *obligatory*.
He posted the *obligatory* photo of his feet on the beach.

position: predicative only — *I felt obliged to help*; never *an obliged friend*
contrast: See *obligated*. *Much obliged* is a slightly old-fashioned, rural-sounding American 'thank you'.

senses.gloss: Having a duty to do something.
examples: I felt *obliged* to say something.
Banks are *obliged* to report large transfers.

senses.gloss: Grateful to someone.
examples: I'd be much *obliged* if you'd take a look at this.
*Much obliged*, ma'am.

position: both — *an obliging neighbor*; *the staff were very obliging*
contrast: Do not confuse it with *obliged* (обязанный). *obliging* describes someone glad to help.

senses.gloss: Willing and eager to help.
examples: The hotel staff were friendly and *obliging*.
An *obliging* stranger helped us carry the suitcase up.
She is always *obliging* when you ask for a favor.

position: both — *an oblique reference*; *his answer was oblique*

senses.gloss: Not said directly; only hinted at.
examples: She made an *oblique* reference to his drinking.
The answer was so *oblique* that nobody understood it.

senses.gloss: Sloping; at an angle that is not a right angle.
examples: The light came in at an *oblique* angle.
Cut the stem at an *oblique* angle before putting it in water.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *he was oblivious to the noise*; also *an oblivious driver*
contrast: It does not mean 'forgetful'. *oblivious to* means failing to notice something that is right in front of you.

senses.gloss: Not noticing what is happening around you.
examples: He walked on, *oblivious* to the traffic around him.
She seemed completely *oblivious* of the effect she had on people.
The kids kept playing, *oblivious* to the rain.

position: both — *an oblong table*; *the room is long and oblong*
contrast: In American use it means longer than it is wide — normally a rectangle. It is also a noun: *cut the dough into oblongs*.

senses.gloss: Longer than it is wide, with straight sides.
examples: They served the cake on an *oblong* platter.
The garden is a narrow *oblong* strip behind the house.
Trace an *oblong* shape on the cardboard and cut it out.

position: both — *an obnoxious guy*; *the music was obnoxious*
contrast: One of the most common American insults for someone loud and rude. Stronger than *annoying*, and about behavior rather than looks.

senses.gloss: Extremely unpleasant, usually in a loud and rude way.
examples: The guy behind us was loud and *obnoxious* the whole game.
He gets *obnoxious* after two beers.
That is the *most obnoxious* ad on television.

position: both — *obscene language*; *the joke was obscene*

senses.gloss: Offensive in a sexual way; indecent.
examples: He was arrested for shouting *obscene* remarks at passersby.
The station was fined for broadcasting *obscene* material.

senses.gloss: So extreme that it is morally shocking — usually about money.
examples: They pay their executives *obscene* bonuses.
The price of a two-bedroom here is *obscene*.

position: both — *an obscure poet*; *the reason remains obscure*
contrast: Also a verb with the same stress: *Clouds obscured the moon*.

senses.gloss: Known by very few people.
examples: He collects records by *obscure* jazz musicians.
She quoted some *obscure* nineteenth-century poet.

senses.gloss: Hard to understand or see clearly.
examples: For reasons that remain *obscure*, the project was canceled.
The instructions were written in the *most obscure* language imaginable.

position: both — *an obsequious waiter*; *he was obsequious to the boss*
contrast: Always negative — flattery too eager to be sincere. Formal; in speech Americans say *fawning* or the blunt *kiss-up*.

senses.gloss: Trying too hard to please someone important.
examples: The waiter's *obsequious* manner made the whole meal uncomfortable.
He is *obsequious* to anyone with money.
She could not stand his *obsequious* emails to the director.

position: both — *an observable change*; *the effect is easily observable*
contrast: *observable* is what can be seen; *observant* is the person doing the seeing.

senses.gloss: Able to be seen or measured.
examples: There was no *observable* difference between the two groups.
The drug produced an *observable* drop in blood pressure.
Science works with what is *observable* and measurable.

position: both — *an observant child*; *she is very observant*
contrast: See *observable*.

senses.gloss: Quick to notice things.
examples: A good nurse has to be *observant*.
She is *more observant* than anyone else in the family.

senses.gloss: Careful to follow the rules and holidays of a religion.
examples: They come from an *observant* Jewish family.
He became *observant* in his thirties.

position: both — *an observational study*; *the evidence is purely observational*
contrast: A research word: an *observational* study only watches, while an experiment changes something. Not the same as *observant*.

senses.gloss: Based on watching rather than on experiment.
examples: The findings come from an *observational* study of 4,000 nurses.
Most of the evidence is *observational*, not experimental.
He does *observational* comedy about everyday life.

position: both — *obsessive behavior*; *he's obsessive about his car*

senses.gloss: Thinking about one thing far too much, in a way you cannot control.
examples: She is *obsessive* about keeping the kitchen clean.
The film shows his *obsessive* need to win.
Checking your phone every minute is *obsessive*.

position: both — *obsessive-compulsive disorder*; *the behavior is obsessive-compulsive*
form: compound — two adjectives joined by a hyphen
contrast: A clinical term, nearly always in the full name *obsessive-compulsive disorder*, shortened to OCD. Calling a tidy friend 'so OCD' is casual slang, not a diagnosis.

senses.gloss: Having unwanted repeated thoughts and the rituals people use to quiet them.
examples: He was diagnosed with *obsessive-compulsive* disorder at fifteen.
Therapy helped her manage the *obsessive-compulsive* rituals.
The clinic specializes in *obsessive-compulsive* and anxiety disorders.

position: both — *obsolete equipment*; *the format is obsolete*
contrast: *obsolete* means no longer used at all. Something merely old-fashioned is *outdated*.

senses.gloss: No longer used, because something better has replaced it.
examples: Fax machines are almost *obsolete* in most offices.
The company still runs on *obsolete* software.
New technology made the whole job *obsolete*.

position: both — *an obstinate child*; *he was obstinate about it*
contrast: Negative, like *stubborn* but more formal. The approving word for the same quality is *determined*.

senses.gloss: Refusing to change your mind, however good the arguments are.
examples: He was *obstinate* and refused to see a doctor.
The talks failed because both sides were *obstinate*.
It is an *obstinate* stain that will not come out of the carpet.

position: both — *an obstreperous crowd*; *the kids got obstreperous*
contrast: Formal and often half-joking. In plain speech Americans say *rowdy* or *unruly*.

senses.gloss: Noisy and difficult to control.
examples: Security removed an *obstreperous* fan from the stands.
The class gets *obstreperous* on the last day before vacation.
He was a loud, *obstreperous* guest at every party.

position: both — *obstructive tactics*; *the agency was obstructive*

senses.gloss: Deliberately getting in the way of something.
examples: The committee accused the agency of being *obstructive*.
He was charged with *obstructive* conduct during the search.

senses.gloss: Blocking a passage in the body — a medical use.
examples: She was treated for *obstructive* sleep apnea.
*Obstructive* lung disease makes breathing out difficult.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *the permit is obtainable online*; also *an easily obtainable drug*

senses.gloss: Able to be got, if you go to the right place.
examples: The forms are *obtainable* from any post office.
The chemical is easily *obtainable* online.
Tickets are *obtainable* only through the box office.

position: both — *an obtrusive camera*; *the ads are obtrusive*
contrast: The negative *unobtrusive* is the more common of the pair: *an unobtrusive waiter*.

senses.gloss: Noticeable in an unwelcome way.
examples: The security cameras are large and *obtrusive*.
He tried to take photos without being *obtrusive*.
The new building is *more obtrusive* than the old one.

position: both — *an obtuse angle*; *don't be obtuse*

senses.gloss: Slow to understand — often said when you suspect the person is pretending.
examples: Stop being deliberately *obtuse*.
He is not stupid, just *obtuse* when it suits him.

senses.gloss: Of an angle: between 90 and 180 degrees.
examples: An *obtuse* angle is wider than a right angle.
Draw a triangle with one *obtuse* angle.

position: attributive only — *an occasional cigarette*; not *the cigarettes are occasional*
contrast: It means 'now and then', not 'по случаю'. Learners more often need the adverb: *I occasionally drink coffee*.

senses.gloss: Happening from time to time, not often or regularly.
examples: She still has an *occasional* cigarette.
We get the *occasional* complaint, but nothing serious.
The forecast is sun with *occasional* showers.

position: attributive only — *occult practices*; after a verb English uses the noun phrase *the occult*
contrast: You will usually meet it as a noun: *an interest in the occult*. Some Americans stress the first syllable: AH-kult.

senses.gloss: Relating to magic and hidden supernatural forces.
examples: The library has a shelf of books on *occult* practices.
He got interested in *occult* symbols as a teenager.
The movie mixes horror with *occult* ritual.

position: attributive only — *occupational therapy*; not *the risk was occupational*
contrast: It means 'to do with your job', not 'skilled'. An *occupational hazard* is a risk that comes with the work.

senses.gloss: Relating to a job and to the risks and training that go with it.
examples: Back pain is an *occupational* hazard for nurses.
She works as an *occupational* therapist.
The agency sets *occupational* safety standards.

position: both — *occupied territory*; *all the seats are occupied*

senses.gloss: In use, so not free.
examples: Every table in the place was *occupied*.
The sign on the restroom door said *occupied*.

senses.gloss: Busy with something.
examples: The puzzle kept the kids *occupied* for an hour.
She is fully *occupied* with the new baby.

senses.gloss: Held by a foreign army.
examples: They grew up in *occupied* territory.
Life in the *occupied* zone was tightly controlled.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *oceanic currents*; *the climate here is oceanic*

senses.gloss: Belonging to or coming from the ocean.
examples: *Oceanic* currents move heat around the planet.
The islands have a mild *oceanic* climate.
She studies *oceanic* food chains.

position: both — *ocher walls*; *the cliffs are ocher*
contrast: American spelling *ocher*; British writing has *ochre*. It is also a noun for the earth pigment itself.

senses.gloss: Of a brownish-yellow color, like the earth pigment.
examples: They painted the kitchen an *ocher* yellow.
The cave walls are covered in *ocher* handprints.
She wore an *ocher* scarf with a gray coat.

position: both — *an octagonal table*; *the tower is octagonal*

senses.gloss: Having eight straight sides.
examples: American stop signs are *octagonal*.
The gazebo has an *octagonal* roof.
They bought an *octagonal* mirror for the hallway.

position: attributive only — *an octogenarian senator*; after a verb English uses the noun
contrast: Much more common as a noun: *a lively octogenarian*. Formal or journalistic either way.

senses.gloss: Between eighty and eighty-nine years old.
examples: The team is coached by an *octogenarian* legend.
Two *octogenarian* senators are running again.
The paper ran a story about an *octogenarian* marathon runner.

position: attributive only — *the odds-on favorite*; American English avoids *he is odds-on*
contrast: Almost always in the fixed phrase *the odds-on favorite*.

senses.gloss: Most likely to win or to happen.
examples: She is the *odds-on* favorite to win the nomination.
The *odds-on* choice lost in the first round.
He went in as the *odds-on* favorite and left with nothing.

position: both — *an odious comparison*; *the practice is odious*
contrast: Formal and strong. Nothing to do with smell — the adjective from *odor* is *odorous*.

senses.gloss: Deserving hatred; extremely unpleasant.
examples: The law was called *odious* by every human rights group.
He made an *odious* comparison between the two events.
It is an *odious* job, but somebody has to do it.

position: both — *an odorless gas*; *the cleaner is odorless*
contrast: American spelling *odorless*; British *odourless*.

senses.gloss: Having no smell.
examples: Carbon monoxide is colorless and *odorless*.
They make an *odorless* version of the paint.
The powder is completely *odorless*.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *the lights are off*; before a noun only in fixed uses: *an off day*, *the off season*
contrast: *off* is far more often a preposition or an adverb (*take it off the shelf*, *he drove off*). It counts as an adjective when it follows *be* or sits in *an off day*.

senses.gloss: Not working; switched off.
examples: Make sure the stove is *off* before you leave.
All the lights were *off* when we got home.

senses.gloss: Canceled; not happening after all.
examples: The wedding is *off*.
If it rains, the game is *off*.

senses.gloss: Below the usual standard; not quite right.
examples: The pitcher was having an *off* day.
Something about his story felt *off*.

position: predicative only — *the question caught me off guard*; never before a noun
contrast: Nearly always after *catch* or *take*. Before a noun English switches words: *an unprepared witness*, not *an off guard witness*.

senses.gloss: Not ready for what happens.
examples: The question caught me completely *off guard*.
The announcement took the whole staff *off guard*.
He was *off guard* for a second, and that was enough.

position: predicative only — *you're off the hook*; never before a noun
contrast: An idiom. The literal sense is a telephone receiver left off its cradle, which is where the figure of speech came from.

senses.gloss: No longer in trouble, or no longer responsible for something.
examples: The check cleared, so you are *off the hook*.
Her confession let the other two *off the hook*.

senses.gloss: Of a telephone: not hung up.
examples: He left the phone *off the hook* all weekend.
The line was busy because the receiver was *off the hook*.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *that's way off-base*; also *an off-base comparison*
form: compound — from baseball, a runner caught *off base*
contrast: American, from baseball, and usually strengthened by *way*: *way off-base*.

senses.gloss: Completely wrong in what you think or say.
examples: Your estimate is way *off-base*.
He apologized and admitted his comment was *off-base*.
That is an *off-base* reading of what she actually said.

position: both — *an off-center design*; *the photo is slightly off-center*
contrast: American spelling *off-center*; British *off-centre*.

senses.gloss: Not exactly in the middle.
examples: The picture hangs a little *off-center*.
An *off-center* part makes the whole wheel wobble.

senses.gloss: A bit odd or unconventional.
examples: The show has a nice *off-center* sense of humor.
He plays the *off-center* neighbor in the sitcom.

position: both — *an off-color joke*; *the humor got off-color*
contrast: American spelling *off-color*. In the US it means mildly indecent. British *off colour* can mean 'unwell', a sense American English does not have.

senses.gloss: Mildly indecent, especially of a joke.
examples: He told an *off-color* joke at the reception.
The comedy special gets *off-color* fast.
Keep the toasts short and nothing *off-color*.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *the second verse was off-key*; also *an off-key note*
contrast: Also a very common adverb: *She sang off-key*.

senses.gloss: Not on the right musical note.
examples: The whole second verse was *off-key*.
He hit an *off-key* note and laughed.

senses.gloss: Striking the wrong tone for the occasion.
examples: His cheerful speech felt *off-key* that day.
The ad campaign struck an *off-key* note.

position: predicative only — *the roof is off-limits*; never before a noun
form: compound — originally the wording on a US military sign

senses.gloss: Not allowed to be entered, used or discussed.
examples: The basement is *off-limits* to guests.
That topic is *off-limits* at dinner.
The beach is *off-limits* after dark.

position: both — *off-line storage*; *the server is off-line*
contrast: Now usually written *offline*, without the hyphen. Also an adverb, and in offices *take this offline* means 'discuss it privately later'.

senses.gloss: Not connected to a network, or not currently running.
examples: The whole system was *off-line* for six hours.
Keep a copy in *off-line* storage.
She keeps her *off-line* life private.

position: both — *an off-putting smell*; *his manner was off-putting*
form: compound — from the phrasal verb *put off*, 'оттолкнуть'

senses.gloss: Unpleasant enough to make you want to keep away.
examples: The smell in the hallway was *off-putting*.
His first email was a little *off-putting*.
Some people find her directness *off-putting*.

position: both — *off-site parking*; *the training is off-site*
contrast: Also an adverb (*the data is stored off-site*) and, in business, a noun: *a two-day off-site*.

senses.gloss: Away from the main building or location.
examples: The hotel offers *off-site* parking for ten dollars a day.
Backups are kept in an *off-site* facility.
Next week's meeting is *off-site*.

position: attributive only — *off-street parking*; not *the parking is off-street*
contrast: You will meet it almost only in apartment listings, in the phrase *off-street parking* — a driveway or lot instead of the curb.

senses.gloss: In a driveway or lot rather than on the public street.
senses.ru: вне проезжей части, на своей парковке
examples: The apartment comes with *off-street* parking.
*Off-street* spaces rent for an extra hundred a month.
The listing mentions two *off-street* spots.

position: both — *an off-the-cuff remark*; *his answer was off-the-cuff*
form: compound — as if reading notes scribbled on a shirt *cuff*
contrast: After a verb it is often written without hyphens, as an adverb: *He spoke off the cuff*.

senses.gloss: Said without preparation.
examples: It was an *off-the-cuff* remark that got him in trouble.
Her answers were *off-the-cuff* but sharp.
He gave an *off-the-cuff* toast at the rehearsal dinner.

position: both — *an off-the-rack suit*; *the jacket is off-the-rack*
contrast: The American phrase for ready-made clothes; the British say *off the peg*. For software and parts the phrase is *off-the-shelf*.

senses.gloss: Bought ready-made in a standard size, not made to measure.
examples: He wore an *off-the-rack* suit to the interview.
*Off-the-rack* sizes never fit him right.
The dress looks expensive, but it is *off-the-rack*.

position: both — *off-the-shelf software*; *the parts are off-the-shelf*
contrast: About products, especially software and parts. For clothes the phrase is *off-the-rack*.

senses.gloss: Ready-made and available to buy, rather than built to order.
examples: They built the site with *off-the-shelf* software.
*Off-the-shelf* parts are much cheaper than custom ones.
Most of the hardware is *off-the-shelf*.

position: both — *an off-the-shoulder dress*; *the neckline is off-the-shoulder*

senses.gloss: Cut to leave the shoulders bare.
senses.ru: с открытыми плечами, со спущенным плечом
examples: She wore an *off-the-shoulder* dress to the wedding.
*Off-the-shoulder* tops are back in style.
The neckline is *off-the-shoulder*.

position: both — *an off-the-wall idea*; *his humor is off-the-wall*
contrast: Informal and usually friendly: strange in an original way, not disturbing.

senses.gloss: Very unusual or eccentric.
examples: He came up with an *off-the-wall* idea that actually worked.
Her sense of humor is completely *off-the-wall*.
The show is the *most off-the-wall* thing on television.

ru: не чисто белый, белый с оттенком
position: both — *off-white walls*; *the paint is off-white*

senses.gloss: White with a faint tint of gray, yellow or cream.
examples: We painted the living room *off-white*.
She chose an *off-white* dress instead of pure white.
The old pages have turned a dingy *off-white*.

position: both — *an offbeat comedy*; *the style is offbeat*
form: compound — from music, a beat that falls *off* the main pulse
contrast: Usually a compliment: unusual in an interesting way. *off-the-wall* is the stronger word.

senses.gloss: Unusual and a little quirky, in a likable way.
examples: It is an *offbeat* comedy about a family of undertakers.
The town has an *offbeat* charm.
She has an *offbeat* way of telling a story.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *she was offended*; also *an offended customer*
contrast: *offended* is what the person feels; *offensive* is what the thing is: *I was offended by the offensive joke*.

senses.gloss: Hurt or angry because of something rude.
examples: She was *offended* by his tone.
Several viewers wrote in, *offended* that the network aired it.
An *offended* customer posted the whole exchange online.

position: both — *an offensive remark*; *the joke was offensive*
contrast: See *offended*. In sports and the military the stress moves to the front: the *AWF-en-siv* line.

senses.gloss: Rude or insulting; causing anger.
examples: The ad was pulled after viewers called it *offensive*.
He apologized for the *offensive* language.

senses.gloss: Used for attacking rather than defending.
examples: They traded for help on the *offensive* line.
The treaty bans *offensive* weapons.

position: both — *an offhand comment*; *he was offhand about it*
contrast: Also a very common adverb meaning 'without checking': *I don't know offhand*. The adjective means casual, sometimes rudely so.

senses.gloss: Said casually, without much thought or care.
examples: It was an *offhand* comment, but it stuck with me.
She was oddly *offhand* about the whole diagnosis.
He gave an *offhand* answer and changed the subject.

position: both — *an offhanded remark*; *his tone was offhanded*
contrast: The same meaning as *offhand*, and the adverb from it, *offhandedly*, is the one Americans reach for most.

senses.gloss: Casual to the point of seeming not to care.
examples: He made an *offhanded* remark about her weight.
Her tone was *offhanded*, almost bored.
The apology felt *offhanded*.

position: both — *the official language*; *the results are official*
contrast: Also a noun: *a city official* (должностное лицо). Do not confuse it with *officious*, which means bossy.

senses.gloss: Approved by a government or organization; formally announced.
examples: Spanish is an *official* language in twenty countries.
The results will not be *official* until Friday.

senses.gloss: Connected with a job or a position of authority.
examples: She was there in an *official* capacity.
He used the *official* car for personal trips.

position: both — *an officious clerk*; *the guard was officious*
contrast: A classic trap. *officious* is not *official*, and not Russian *официозный*. It describes a minor official who enjoys giving orders.

senses.gloss: Too eager to use a small amount of authority.
examples: An *officious* clerk made us fill out the form three times.
The guard was *officious* about the parking rules.
He becomes *officious* the moment you hand him a clipboard.

position: both — *offshore drilling*; *the accounts are offshore*

senses.gloss: In the sea, at a distance from the coast.
examples: The state approved two *offshore* wind farms.
*Offshore* drilling has been banned along that coast.

senses.gloss: Placed in another country, usually to pay less tax.
examples: The money sat in an *offshore* account for years.
They moved the whole support team *offshore*.

position: both — *oily skin*; *the sauce tastes oily*

senses.gloss: Covered in oil, or containing a lot of it.
examples: He wiped his *oily* hands on a rag.
This fish is *oilier* than salmon.

senses.gloss: Too smooth and flattering to be trusted — of a person.
examples: The salesman had an *oily* charm.
There was something *oily* about his compliments.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *are you okay?*; also *an okay movie*
contrast: Also spelled *OK*. The same word works as an adjective (*the food was okay*), an adverb (*she did okay*), a noun (*I need your okay*) and a verb (*the board okayed it*).

senses.gloss: Unhurt, healthy or safe.
examples: Are you *okay*? That was a hard fall.
The kids are *okay*, just shaken up.

senses.gloss: Acceptable, but no better than that.
examples: The movie was *okay*, nothing special.
Is it *okay* if I bring a friend?

position: attributive only — *old-time music*; not *the music is old-time*
contrast: Warm and nostalgic, never an insult. The related *old-timer* is a noun for a longtime member or an old man.

senses.gloss: Belonging to or in the style of an earlier time.
examples: They play *old-time* fiddle music at the festival.
The diner has an *old-time* feel.
He believes in *old-time* religion.

position: attributive only — *old-world charm*; not *the hotel is old-world*
form: compound — from *the Old World*, meaning Europe
contrast: Usually a compliment about European-style charm and manners. Capitalized, *the Old World* is a noun for Europe, Asia and Africa.

senses.gloss: Having the charm and courtesy associated with old Europe.
examples: The hotel has a certain *old-world* charm.
He greeted her with *old-world* courtesy.
The café is full of *old-world* details — brass, velvet and dark wood.

position: attributive only — *the olfactory nerve*; not *the sense is olfactory*

senses.gloss: Relating to the sense of smell.
examples: The *olfactory* nerve carries signals from the nose to the brain.
The virus damaged her *olfactory* system.
Perfumers train their *olfactory* memory for years.

position: both — *an olive jacket*; *the walls are olive*
contrast: As a color it is a dark yellow-green. But *olive skin* means a warm light-brown complexion, not a green one. The fruit *olive* is a noun.

senses.gloss: Of a dull yellowish-green color; of skin, warm light brown.
examples: He wore an *olive* jacket and jeans.
She has dark hair and *olive* skin.
The bedroom walls are a soft *olive* green.

position: both — *Olympian calm*; *his detachment was Olympian*
form: from *Olympus*, the mountain of the Greek gods
contrast: Also a noun for an athlete who competes in the Games: *a three-time Olympian*. The adjective for the Games themselves is *Olympic*.

senses.gloss: Calm and superior, as a god looking down on human affairs.
examples: She watched the argument with *Olympian* calm.
He wrote with an *Olympian* detachment from ordinary life.
The judges kept an *Olympian* distance from the press.

position: attributive only — *an Olympic medal*; not *the medal is Olympic*
form: from *Olympia*, where the ancient games were held
contrast: *Olympic* is for the Games; *Olympian* is for the gods, or a noun for an athlete competing.

senses.gloss: Relating to the Olympic Games.
examples: She won an *Olympic* gold medal in Tokyo.
The pool is *Olympic* size.
He trains with the *Olympic* team.

position: both — *Omani oil*; *most of the crew were Omani*
contrast: Also a noun for a person from Oman: *two Omanis*. Nationality words are always capitalized in English.

senses.gloss: From or relating to Oman.
examples: The *Omani* government signed the agreement.
We ate at an *Omani* restaurant in Dearborn.
Most of the crew were *Omani*.

position: both — *an ominous silence*; *the sky looked ominous*

senses.gloss: Suggesting that something bad is about to happen.
examples: There was an *ominous* silence on the other end of the line.
Dark, *ominous* clouds moved in from the west.
The last paragraph of the memo was *ominous*.

position: attributive only — *an omnibus bill*; not *the bill is omnibus*
contrast: In American news this almost always means one large bill or book that packs many separate items together. The old sense 'bus' survives only in British English.

senses.gloss: Covering many separate items in a single package.
examples: Congress passed an *omnibus* spending bill at the last minute.
The *omnibus* edition collects all three novels.
Lawmakers buried the change in an *omnibus* package.

position: both — *an omnipotent god*; *the state is not omnipotent*

senses.gloss: Having unlimited power.
examples: They believe in an *omnipotent* and loving God.
The company acts as though it were *omnipotent*.
No government is *omnipotent*.

position: both — *the omnipresent cameras*; *advertising is omnipresent*

senses.gloss: Present everywhere at once.
examples: Security cameras are *omnipresent* in the airport.
The *omnipresent* hum of traffic never stops.
Her phone is *omnipresent*, even at dinner.

position: both — *an omniscient narrator*; *the narrator is omniscient*
contrast: Most Americans meet this word in the literature classroom: an *omniscient* narrator knows every character's thoughts.

senses.gloss: Knowing everything.
examples: The novel is told by an *omniscient* narrator.
Nobody on the committee is *omniscient*.
The story shifts from first person to *omniscient*.

position: both — *an omnivorous animal*; *bears are omnivorous*
contrast: Also used figuratively about appetites of the mind: *an omnivorous reader*.

senses.gloss: Eating both plants and meat.
examples: Bears are *omnivorous* — they eat berries and fish.
Humans are an *omnivorous* species.
She was an *omnivorous* reader, finishing three books a week.

position: predicative only — *the lights are on*; *the game is still on*
contrast: *on* is overwhelmingly a preposition (*on the table*) or an adverb (*keep going on*). It is an adjective only after *be*, meaning 'working' or 'happening as planned'.

senses.gloss: Working; switched on.
examples: The oven is *on*.
Leave the porch light *on*.

senses.gloss: Happening as planned.
examples: The concert is still *on* despite the rain.
Dinner at seven — are we still *on*?

position: both — *on-site parking*; *the nurse is on-site*
contrast: Also an adverb: *The engineer works on-site three days a week*.

senses.gloss: Located at the place where the work or activity happens.
examples: The building has an *on-site* gym and laundry.
There is an *on-site* manager for emergencies.
All of the training is *on-site*.

ru: без отрыва от производства, на рабочем месте
position: attributive only — *on-the-job training*; not *the training is on-the-job*
contrast: Almost always *on-the-job training* or *an on-the-job injury*. After a verb the hyphens drop: *He was injured on the job*.

senses.gloss: Happening at work, while you are doing the work.
examples: The company provides two weeks of *on-the-job* training.
She filed a claim for an *on-the-job* injury.
Most of what he knows came from *on-the-job* experience.

position: attributive only — *an on-the-spot fine*; not *the fine was on-the-spot*
contrast: Without hyphens it is an adverb phrase: *They fined him on the spot*. The idiom *put someone on the spot* means to force a hard answer.

senses.gloss: Done immediately, right where the situation is.
examples: Officers can issue an *on-the-spot* fine.
She was hired in an *on-the-spot* decision.
The network filed an *on-the-spot* report from the scene.

position: attributive only — *oncoming traffic*; not *the traffic was oncoming*
contrast: Above all a driving word: *oncoming traffic* is the traffic coming toward you.

senses.gloss: Moving toward you.
examples: He drifted into the *oncoming* lane.
Dim your headlights for *oncoming* traffic.
She stepped back from the *oncoming* crowd.

position: attributive only — *a one-armed man*; not *the man is one-armed*
contrast: The pattern number + noun + *-ed* builds many adjectives: *two-story*, *four-door*, *one-eyed*. A slot machine is a *one-armed bandit*.

senses.gloss: Having only one arm.
examples: The story is about a *one-armed* pitcher who made the majors.
He can do a *one-armed* pull-up.
Casinos used to be full of *one-armed* bandits.

position: both — *a one-dimensional character*; *the villain is one-dimensional*

senses.gloss: Having no depth — of people, characters or arguments.
examples: The villain is *one-dimensional* and never becomes interesting.
His view of the city is *one-dimensional*.

senses.gloss: Having only one dimension — in math and physics.
examples: A line is a *one-dimensional* object.
The model reduces the flow to a *one-dimensional* problem.

position: attributive only — *a one-eyed cat*; not *the cat is one-eyed*
contrast: Built like *one-armed*. The proverb runs: in the land of the blind, the *one-eyed* man is king.

senses.gloss: Having only one eye.
examples: They adopted a *one-eyed* cat from the shelter.
He drew a *one-eyed* monster on the napkin.
In the land of the blind, the *one-eyed* man is king.
